utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing will commence. Could Mr. Registrar call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, our assistant, Mathias Neuner, and Kimberly Fleming, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and all those present in the courtroom. We'll continue with the examination of a witness. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, with regard to the schedule for the following week, it has been confirmed that the hearing on Tuesday will be cancelled, so that we will be sitting on Wednesday all day, in the morning and in the afternoon. I hope that won't exhaust you. But as everyone will have the opportunity to have a rest on Tuesday, you will be in very good shape for Wednesday, since we'll be starting at 9.00 and the hearing will be concluded at 7.00 p.m. We'll have two hearings, one after the other, more or less, but we will have the usual breaks. Unless the schedule is changed in the meantime, and we'll be informed of that on Monday. The Prosecution will ensure that the witnesses scheduled for Tuesday will be ready to be examined on Wednesday, if that is necessary. With regard to the video footage, the Judges have deliberated. At this point in time, it is the opinion of the Judges that the relevance can be established on the basis of the contents of the video itself. And in addition, according to the Prosecution, this video relates to events of which the victim was -- of which the witness was a victim. If the evidence is not reliable, it has to be rejected. That is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. And this was the case in a number of cases. For example, in Celebici. If evidence is not reliable and decisions are taken to reject such evidence. But given that the witness himself can provide information, will enable us to determine the nature of the video, to determine whether this element, the element of reliability, is one that can be counted on. We'll now continue with the examination-in-chief, and we will be viewing the video footage. Naturally, it's necessary to make a distinction between the admissibility of evidence and its probative weight. If a document is admissible, this does not mean that it is being given probative weight, because the Judges will subsequently deliberate on the basis of the documents, on the basis of the testimony of witnesses, and on the basis of other elements that will be obtained through other testimony or other evidence. Admissibility does not automatically imply that the document in question has probative value. Probative value will be determined by the Judges, who will assess all the relevant elements. Yes, Mr. Withopf, would you like to make any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I wish to provide additional information on this video footage. For that purpose, however, I would like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can I please, again, ask the usher to remove the ELMO, since I can't see the witness properly. Thank you very much. Mr. President, Your Honours, as announced and discussed, the Prosecution will now show a video. It's about five minutes. And the Prosecution will have a number of questions afterwards to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you will see the video on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, after having seen this video footage, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what one can see on this video footage.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the vehicle I was in, and that was attacked on the 15th of April. Ivica Vidovic was the driver. When the shooting started, he was the first one to be hit and he fell over me. At the back, Marko Ljubic, one of the escorts, was sitting there; Tihomir Ljubic, another escort, was in the middle; and to the right, at the back, my wife's brother, Anto Zrnic, was there. After my escort had said that Marko should run out and my wife's brother should protect me, he wanted the window to be opened. The shooting then broke out. A couple of bullets were fired from my vehicle. And there was intense firing at the vehicle and the wheels. This all took place very rapidly. So the escort, Marko Ljubic, opened the door and tried to jump out. I don't think he even managed to jump out. He was immediately cut down by a burst of fire. I opened the door and tried to get out. I was still on the seat, but my head and shoulders were protruding outside. I took my pistol out, and that's when I felt a severe blow to my head and to my arm. I then dropped my pistol. I was dragged out of the vehicle and put into a vehicle. I think it was a van. A bag was put over my head, and we drove off at great speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then heard a burst of fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, may I please stop you here. From what you could see on the video, was this the exact scene of your kidnapping and the killing of your escort?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier on, Mr. Totic, that you'd seen four people attacking the car. Can you please describe or can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether these people wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the vehicle stopped about 10 metres from my vehicle, four soldiers got out very fast. They were at the front. And two were to the left of the vehicle. They were all in uniforms, and at the time the BH army wore such uniforms. They all had masks on, and they were wearing gloves, apart from one person, who during my detention and when negotiations were in course, I think that this person participated in the attack and was also involved in the exchange and had something to do with the place where I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Totic. Having seen the video footage and having been the victim of this kidnapping, and based on your knowledge -- your knowledge in military terms, would you describe -- or how would you describe this action was done? Was it done in a professional manner, if one can describe such an action as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The question put to the witness was one that the Prosecution had already given us a foreknowledge of. Mr. President, we think that this question and such questions shouldn't be allowed, because the witness before us is a factual witness and we are asking him to give us his opinion. Mr. President, we have already made certain submissions before this Trial Chamber with regard to the reasons for which opinions should not be admitted. First of all, because when expressing opinions, you need special skills. The opinion may not be objective or precise, exact. Secondly, testifying about opinions is up to the Chamber. The Chamber is in a position to decide about the evidence and on the basis of the video. Thirdly, there's the danger of asking the witness to testify with regard to facts and also to express his opinion about the same facts. And fourthly, with regard to the procedure that is well established in this Tribunal in the Rules, when we want to receive expert testimony, naturally the experts' report has to be filed and then the opposing party, either the Defence or the Prosecution, can make submissions with regard to the report. And the Trial Chamber will then lender a decision on this basis and will decide about admissibility or whether an expert is authorised to express his opinions. These criteria, Mr. President, are elaborated in detail in a decision in the Delalic case, number IT - standing for International Tribunal - 96-21-T, for trial. This decision is entitled "Decision on the motion by the Prosecution to allow the investigators to follow the trial during the testimonies of witnesses." In this decision, it is -- a clear distinction is made between expert testimony and factual testimony. What is more important in this case, Mr. President, in the opinion of the Defence, is that the nature of the present case is such that many military experts will be testifying before this Chamber. These witnesses do in fact possess special skills, special military skills. These witnesses will be coming from a number of countries. They will have different ranks. They will have had different experiences. If the Trial Chamber allows this witness -- these witnesses to express their opinion, then the position will be more difficult because the Trial Chamber may be faced with an opinion that could be expressed by 20 witnesses, and that is the difficulty that has to be assessed by the Trial Chamber. Are they to allow 20 opinions, rather than to allow for factual testimony? Because on the basis of the facts expressed by these witnesses, the Trial Chamber will be able to assess the situation. And it is for these reasons that in future such questions which concern the witness's opinion shouldn't be allowed in the case of this witness and in the case of future witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, you've taken note of the comments made. I'll summarise the Defence's position. With regard to a witness testifying about the facts, of which was a victim or which he witnessed, it is not in the Defence's opinion possible to ask such a witness for his opinion. He is only asked to testify about what happened and not to express his subjective opinion. Opinions can only be subjective. The Defence also mentioned that, with regard to opinions -- well, it is for expert witnesses to express their opinions. In general, with regard to military opinions, there are no -- there's no contestation, because the Defence objects to a witness expressing opinion, because this is a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide. What is your position before we rule on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, very briefly. Of course Mr. Totic is a fact witness and not an expert witness. However, Mr. Totic was the victim of this kidnapping. He knows about the facts, and he already testified extensively in respect to the facts of this kidnapping. Each and every fact witness can draw conclusions, conclusions based on the facts. That doesn't make him to an expert. And in particular, the witness Totic has the relevant and the respective skill set taking into account his long military career, which he informed the Chamber of yesterday in great detail. Therefore, the Prosecution is of the view that Mr. Totic can be asked such questions which are nothing else but asking him to draw conclusions based on the facts and based on things he personally experienced and went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are going to retire to deliberate. However, I am coming back to the question that was asked, and the question was whether this operation, according to you, was carried out in a professional manner. That was the sense of the question, and this is what the Prosecution wanted to know, and they asked you in your capacity as a soldier whether you as a soldier are familiar with the operation of this type. We are going to retire, and we are going to come back in a couple of minutes. Please don't leave. --- Break taken at 9.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The Chamber has deliberated on the position of the Prosecution that they should be allowed to put this question. The Chamber has taken note of the fact that the question deals with a technical issue and it consistent in asking the witness, who was the victim of a kidnapping, whether the operation carried out by the perpetrators was carried out in a professional way. Since it is a technical question and the witness is a military person and he can answer, the question is going to be considered a technical question and the witness may answer, providing, Mr. Withopf, that you put the question in such a way that you make it a technical question, that you don't ask for the witness's opinion. You don't have an expert in front of you. This is a factual witness. And when it -- when you have an expert witness, then you have to provide a written opinion in advance. But now we are dealing with a technical issue, and in that sense the witness may provide an answer, providing you can rephrase your question along these lines. Ask him about the technical details. Witness, you are going to ask -- you are going to answer this question as a technical expert on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, an action of such a magnitude, what sort of planning and logistics are involved in carrying it out?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, such an operation has to be carefully planned in advance, and it must have been carried out by professionals. The weapons involved in the attack that the perpetrators used was not available to every unit. The equipment that they had was -- are such as can be found in military police units, because other units don't have handcuffs. After the kidnapping, the treatment that I was given made me conclude that the group consisted of highly disciplined people who have a very structured command. And when I was interrogated, I could conclude from the questions that the people were very highly skilled and knowledgeable in military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, can you please again tell us where exactly the kidnapping and the killing of your escort happened.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the kidnapping took place in the Pobrijezje village sector, some 50 metres away from the crossroads between Pobrijezje and Detevo [phoen], 1 kilometre and 400 metres away from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber in which town your apartment was located at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, my apartment was in Travnicka Street, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, based on what you've just said about the planning and logistics and the necessary skill sets of the people who carry out such an action, can it be done without the knowledge of the military power in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution was authorised by the Chamber to ask questions that will belong to the scope of technical matters and call for an answer that will pertain to technical sphere. And now this question goes beyond what has been authorised by the Chamber. During our cross-examination, we shall have an opportunity to address that issue. And now we are going to -- we are going beyond the technical issue and we have to know now -- we want to -- the witness was asked whether this operation required knowledge of military power in the region. I believe that this question, Mr. President, goes beyond military knowledge and calls for a subjective opinion which may arise from the relationship between a victim and a participant in the event, and we would like to Chamber not to allow this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, before I give you the floor, you have asked the witness whether this operation, military operation, could have been carried out without extensive military knowledge. Was that the sense, the gist of your question? At this moment, with your question what you are trying to establish is whether the persons who carried out this attack - this is, at least, the Chamber's opinion - this question connects the personality of the witness and what happened to him. And the question is whether the attack could have been carried out within the framework of extensive military knowledge? Is that the sense of your question? Because the Defence formally objects to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the question is actually a slightly different one, and I'll repeat it from the transcript: Can such an action be done without the knowledge of the military power in the area? And again, I wish to emphasise that Mr. Totic has the necessary skill set based on his own very long career and based on his position at the time and later on and his high rank to provide the Chamber information on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to retire to deliberate for a couple of minutes. We shall be back shortly. --- Break taken at 9.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to render our oral decision whether the Prosecution may ask this question. The Chamber is of the opinion that the response that may be given to this question will have only speculative value to the extent it is going to be an opinion of the witness, because this response will rely on other elements that allow to describe the conditions in which this operation took place. So since this is going to be an opinion, the Chamber is aware of that and the Chamber rules that the question shouldn't [as interpreted] be allowed. The Chamber would then like to ask you to ask the question and rephrase it. You can ask the question rephrasing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, yesterday you already informed the Trial Chamber what happened after the actual kidnapping. Can you please tell us for how long you were detained.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was detained from 15 April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am coming back to the previous issue. In the English transcript, it says that the Chamber will not allow the question. However, that is not what I said. I said that -- this is line 17, page 15 of the transcript. The Chamber has authorised the Prosecution to ask the question but the response is going to be considered an opinion response, which in itself will contain other elements complementary to the response. And the Chamber does authorise the Prosecution to ask the question, but if the Prosecution wants to withdraw the question, of course they can withdraw it. We would like to avoid any ambiguities. Mr. Withopf, you are authorised to ask the question; however, the Chamber will understand that it is just an opinion when the witness gives his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, I'm now going to ask you the question again. Can such an action - and I am referring to the kidnapping, your kidnapping, and the killing of your escort - can it be done without the knowledge of the military power in the area? And the area is Zenica.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the kidnapping was carried out by well-trained professional special forces, in my opinion, which in my opinion should be positioned in the military police - and it is well known that the 3rd Corps of the BH army had on its strength a military police battalion which was directly subordinated to the commander of the 3rd Corps - I believe that this could not have been done without the knowledge of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you are saying, this is just your personal opinion. There are no elements on which you could base that and say that it is a fact. It is your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only my opinion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about technicalities of the issue, you saw the video. We saw that there were bursts of fire coming from the front, from the back, and from the left side of the vehicle. We saw the bullet holes, and this means that those who were shooting were very close to the vehicle and the -- the way the victims looked means that they could have been saved only by a miracle. When it comes to other technical issues, you were not killed because I -- I conclude that they were shooting from the left; you were sitting on the right. We do not know that. We can only conclude. And the person who was on the right was also shooting, but you could not have been killed. When it comes to this -- these technical matters, given the number of bullets, the number of perpetrators, was this really an operation that was carried out by special forces or was that a situation from which you escaped although they were shooting at you? At a technical level, what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe - and I'm convinced - that this was done by special forces, by specially trained forces. One bullet was fired and killed the driver. At the moment when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the escort Ljubic, Marko Ljubic, tried to jump out of the vehicle, he was cut directly. He was hit directly. So there was no fire opened from the flanks. Only after that two perpetrators hit the back seat. So there was just one shot fired at the driver. When I managed to get out of the vehicle, I heard a burst of fire which lasted for half a minute. I'm just giving my opinion. I suppose that at that moment they came closer. After I read the on-site investigation notes carried out by the military police of the Security Services Centre in Zenica, I saw in the investigation report that the escorts' arms, pistols, had been collected and the helmets were in the back. None of that was there before. I believe that the kidnappers had collected the weapons and the rest of the equipment and then carried out the massacre that was seen as the final result. To corroborate this effect, I can say that according to the same on-site report, another eyewitness to the event was also murdered. He was a Muslim, a father of a 16-year-old child. His name is Avdaga Doglod. It is assumed that he was murdered, shot at from the vehicle, that after the incident the perpetrators took over and drove away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Before I continue with asking additional questions to the witness, Mr. President, in respect to tendering the video sequence into evidence, we are facing the very same situation as in respect to the last video footage. This video footage is a portion of a longer videotape, and in compliance with the guidance given by the Chamber, very well, we have to isolate the portion. We have to remove the audio. And we have to burn it on CD. It will be tendered in the course of next week. However, if possible, I wish already today to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P69, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P69, marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, again I know you already answered it, but can you please rephrase it. For how long were you detained?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was detained from the 15th of April, 1993 until the 17th of April, 1993 [as interpreted]. So 33 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There may or may not be a translation mistake in the transcript. It says "from the 15th of April until the 17th of April, 1993." When were you released, Mr. Totic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 17th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Totic, for this clarification. For the 33 days, have you always been detained in the same facility?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, during those 33 days, they moved me on five or six occasions to different locations. The first location I was detained in, I only spent one night there. On the 16th, in the evening, they transferred me to a nearby house, which was about 50 metres away. I spent the night there. I slept on a couch. I wasn't even able to stretch myself out on it. And on another couch - the area was small - there was another person who almost spent the entire night with me. Throughout that period of time, I was blindfolded. And when they brought me food, they wanted me to eat with the blindfold on. I spent one day at that location, and on the 17th of April they moved me to a location which was about 10 or 15 minutes away. We went there on foot. On the basis of the terrain we went through, I came to the conclusion that we were going uphill. But they often asked me to look down. So I really don't know whether these were just tricks they were using to confuse me. They took me into the room of a house. When I sat down -- they ordered me to sit down. They took the black bag off my head. I saw that I was in a room. There was a wall to the left. To the right, there was the back of a piece of furniture. I couldn't even turn around easily. I was only able to sleep on my left side, as my head had been injured. I wasn't able to sleep on my right side. The kidnappers kept me there until about the 13th or 14th of May. They told me that I would be exchanged. They then transferred me either to the town or somewhere near the town. I don't know whether it was a military facility or a school that they transferred me to. I couldn't say for sure, but that's where I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can I stop you here for a moment, please, Mr. Totic. You were repeatedly making reference to people who were present during your detention. Who are actually the people you are referring to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were mostly present while I was detained, the person who participated in the kidnapping. I think there was some central figure there as one whose face was shown. But because of the person's complexion, you could conclude that the person was of Arabic origin. After I'd been taken to this first location, and after I'd been taken to the basement, about 15 or 20 minutes later he turned up not in military uniform. He was wearing clothes that Arabs wear, some sort of a tunic. He introduced himself, said he was a doctor, and he examined my wound. He reappeared at the next location. He brought a lady with him, who examined me and prescribed some medicine for me. And during my exchange, this person could be seen very well. And at the exchange, I said, "How are you, Doctor?" And he very angrily replied, "I'm not a doctor."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you are just making reference to a person of Arabic origin. In which language or languages did the people who guarded you, in which languages did they talk to each other?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who stood guard while I was in detention - and at night I couldn't sleep because I was afraid that they would kill me during the night - they would speak until late into the night. First they would check to see whether I was sleeping. I pretended that I was. In fact, I was eavesdropping. While I was there, I was able to conclude that there were Arabs there but also quite a lot of people who spoke the local language. I'd like to point out that only one person would approach me and would show his face, and maybe about ten days later an Arab also turned up. He showed his face, and I spoke to him. All the others, even when they would bring me food, wore masks. But even then one could conclude that when the Arabs brought food -- they didn't have gloves on. But I assumed that the local people, when they brought food in, if they didn't have any gloves on they would use rags to wrap their hands up, probably to prevent them from being identified as local people on the basis of their complexion, on the basis of the colour of their skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, moving on to some significance event -- significant events during your detention. Did there come a time when you were interrogated in the course of your detention?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interrogated on two occasions. I think the first time was after three or four days had passed. A man appeared. I assumed it was a politician because he didn't ask me any questions of a military nature. He used a sort of electronic device to distort his voice, and naturally he was masked. He was masked; you couldn't see his face. They took the bag off my head. He asked me some questions, mostly questions about political and military figures in Zenica and in its surroundings. He asked me what I thought about the chief of the municipality, what I thought about the HVO president, what I thought about Mr. Saric, the Territorial Defence commander, what I thought about Fuad Dzidic, the president of the SDA; Josip Pojavnik, the president of the HDZ, and so on. That was the first interrogation. The second time I was interrogated, the questions had to do with military matters. They came and ordered me to stand up. They put a cap on my head. They sorted out the jacket I was wearing, and they said I had to give a statement that they were to forward to HVO representatives for an exchange. They also said that they wanted to exchange me but that my people didn't want me. They took me to another room behind the piece of furniture. I saw that it was a narrow room. There was a small window, a typical Bosnian window, and there was one door. There was a camera in front, and there was a chair at the back and I sat down on that chair. They asked me to give a statement then, and they asked me to address the political and military leadership of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and they asked me to request that they have me exchanged for Mujahedin, that is to say, for foreigners who were in the prisons of Herceg-Bosna. After that event -- well, they also told me that I could greet close family members on that occasion there. Then I wanted to go to sleep, because I had a headache, but then they said, "The main thing is about to happen." Now they moved the chair. They made me kneel down on the floor. A short man who was masked approached me. He sat opposite me, at the other end of the room, and he started interrogating me. First of all, a map was shown to me. One -- the scale was 1 to 50.000. I was familiar with the map. It was in my command in the meetings hall. Nothing else was marked on the map, apart from the zone of responsibility. And it contained military symbols. It was between the Jure Francetic Brigade and the 314th BH. There were another two details, artillery locations, 120-millimetre mortar sites had been marked, and anti-aircraft guns, 20 through 3 millimetres. And naturally, I was familiar with those locations. The first question put to me was: Is this the border between Herceg-Bosna? I said, "That's ridiculous." I said, "There aren't any borders. That's just a map symbol which has been marked in accordance with the military rules as well as the zone of responsibility separating brigades." He said I was lying. He then continued interrogating me, and the questions he asked showed that he was very familiar with military terms and with weapons. He didn't ask me about weapons in my brigade because the brigade I was in command of was only being founded at the time. It was pretty badly equipped. I was mostly asked about the weapons possessed in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. He asked me how many tanks we had, how many carriers, how many 152-millimetre Howitzers or, rather, Noras. When I told him I didn't know the answer to that question, one man got up, gave me a karate kick to the chest, and I fell down on my back. Then I think an Arab jumped up and hit that person. He said that the detainee was not to be beaten. And after that, no one hit me again while I was in detention. The questioning continued. And when I said I didn't know how many weapons there were, he said, "Answer the questions, one or two." And I said, "One or two." When I didn't say we didn't have any Noras, he said, "What do you mean you don't have Noras, since they are shelling Zenica from Kavarija" Your Honours, I'd like to repeat here that at the time I really did not know how many Noras we had, nor did I know the location of these Noras.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, may I please stop you here. Sorry. During the interrogation, did there come a time when the interpreters -- the interrogators identified themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no one identified themselves, but the interrogation was quite tortuous. Before the interrogation, they bought a metre and a half of explosive fuse, 100 grams of trotile, which was connected to a detonator, 2 and a half metres of cables, electric cables, and in his other hand he had a battery, a 4 and a half volt battery, which was used to detonate. He said, "You know if you wrap this around, it can cut through 20 centimetres of wood." I said I knew that. They then put this around my neck, and that's how they interrogated me. When I had had enough of everything, I tried to approach the detonating device, but then this person jumped back from me and then about a minute or two later they interrupted the interrogation. They were probably -- they probably feared for their own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, even if the interrogators didn't identify themselves with their names, did there come a time when they revealed to which military unit, if any, they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the end of the interrogation I was told, "Do you know who kidnapped you?" I said I didn't. They said, "If you reveal this, if you say who kidnapped you, you and your people, those closest to you, will be killed." And I was then told that a company of the special military police belonging to the 3rd Corps had kidnapped me." Your Honours, I'm telling you what I was told at the time, so I can't guarantee you that that was the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you were informing the Trial Chamber that at one occasion a military map was discussed, and you actually made reference that it was your map from your command. Was it your impression or did you know or do you know that the map that was shown to you was the map you used in your command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it really was the map that we used in my command, and I believe - and at the time I believed - that someone had betrayed me and taken that map away. I started sweating at that time. However, in my opinion, after four or five days - I think it was on the 25th of May that I was interrogated. After the conflict in Zenica, a certain unit came in, took the map, and brought it. I think that is proof that 3rd Corps forces also participated in my kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The individuals who interrogated you, based on the questions they asked you, did you get the impression that they were informed about the military situation within the ABiH 3rd Corps at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the basis of the questions that they asked me, yes, that is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, since I now intend to ask the witness a number of questions in relation to his exchange and we are very close to the break, may I suggest to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We will now adjourn. It is almost half past 10.00. We'll resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you already mentioned half an hour ago that there came a time when you were exchanged. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber how it was organised, where took place, and who was present during the exchange.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my exchange was carried out on the 17th of May, 1993 in the centre of town, in front of the Internacional Hotel. The Internacional Hotel is to the left from the stadium, some 150 metres as the crow flies from the command of the 3rd Corps. Representatives of the European Monitoring Mission participated in my exchange. There were also uniformed personnel in white uniforms such as were worn by the army members at the time. They didn't have any insignia. I didn't notice any insignia. There was a person whose face was uncovered, and he wore Arabic uniform. That was the doctor who introduced himself to me when I was kidnapped and when he examined the wound on my head. In addition to them, on the right-hand side I saw the vehicle that they came in. I saw some people standing there. And I also saw people with the insignia. I couldn't see the insignia, but I could see patches on their shoulders. They wore BH army uniforms, and I suppose that they provided security for the exchange venue. They were mixed with the civilians, and they were standing a bit further from the place of the exchange. The act of exchange itself lasted for some two or three hours. After some negotiation and talks, a representative of the European Monitoring Mission approached me, asked to identify me. My commander at the time approached a British APC. The APC was reversing and it approached the vehicle where I was. The door was open, and among other people I saw Colonel Zvonko Vukovic in the APC. He was one of the assistant commanders in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. After that, the door closed and the vehicle drove off. After that, when the act of exchange began, I was told that I would be transferred to another vehicle. Before that, the blindfolds were taken off from our eyes, and in the vehicle just before I came there I saw two other people sitting in the same vehicle with me. They were civilians. One of them I knew. When all the soldiers left the vehicle, I asked him where he was from and where could I know him from. He told me that he worked at the radio station, the owner of which was my acquaintance, Zoran Misetic and this guy worked for him. I asked him where he was captured. He said it was either on the same day or the day after I was kidnapped. They came to the -- see the radio. He was also kidnapped and taken to an unknown place. The exchange itself was supervised by the European monitors, who were standing on the left and on the right side to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, it appears to be pretty obvious, since you said the exchange took place some 150 metres as the crow flies from the 3rd Corps headquarters, and you mentioned the town. Which town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I intend to now show the witness a further video, and I will provide additional information on this video. For that purpose, could we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, the Prosecution is now going to show you a second videotape. It will again appear on the screen in front of you. And I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Totic, to the people being present during the exchange. I will ask you a number of questions after you've seen the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the wrong one. There will be another one. I apologise. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you have seen on this video.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could see the vehicle in which I was brought for the exchange to the centre of town in front of the Internacional Hotel. To my right side in the vehicle, there was a Croat. I believe that his name was Ante Antunovic, but I am not sure. And on the left, there was this young lad, who was one of the -- of the anchors at Mr. Misetic's private radio station in Zenica. The persons who jumped out of the vehicle were masked all the time. And while they were sitting with me in the vehicle and when our blindfolds were taken off, I could see that they were mixed. When looking at their hands, I could see that some of them were locals and that the others were foreigners. The person in Arabic uniform is the person that introduced himself as a doctor, who in my opinion - and I'm convinced of that - was involved in the act of kidnapping itself. Later on, while I was imprisoned, he was also there and he was the person in charge during the exchange. He was the one who negotiated with the international monitors. He went to the third and fourth floor at the Internacional Hotel, where negotiations were taking place regarding the exchange. So he was the central, the key figure in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Totic, could you see any regular ABiH soldiers being present during the exchange?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could clearly see that they were regular ABiH soldiers standing together with the civilians. They were lined up in the way guards usually secure a public event. This made me conclude that this exchange was organised by the military authorities that were in charge at the time in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the military authorities that were in charge at the time in Zenica were which military authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the leading military authority was the commander of the highest formation, and that was the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Totic, for whom you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, while I was detained, they told me that I was not a problem, that there are others who are a problem. They are allegedly members of the HVO who were robbing their brethren Muslims who came to defend local Muslims. And they told me also they didn't ask for anything else but for all their brethren imprisoned all over Bosnia-Herzegovina to be released. They told me that some were kept in Kaonik, and they also told me they were aware of the fact that one of them was dead. After the exchange, I learnt something that I didn't know beforehand; I didn't know whether there were any foreign nationals in prisons. I know that I did not participate in the arrest and detention of any foreign citizen, not a single one. Later on I found out that 11 or 12 people were exchanged for me. They were also brought to the centre of Zenica in front of the Internacional Hotel once I had already left. The act of exchange, according to my information that I later on received from the international monitors, the vehicles crossed the separation line at the same time and went off towards Kaonik on the Zenica-Busovaca road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The 11 or 12 people that were exchanged for you, were they Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were all Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the situation with this video footage is the same as with the previous one; it only forms part of a far longer video. We again have to isolate the respective portion, to burn it on CD. We will tender it into evidence in the course of next week; however, we wish to get a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any other questions regarding this videotape, or are you going to move on? The Chamber would like to seek a clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I intend to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Witness, we have seen the video. The Defence has seen it as well. We can see you arriving at the central square. We can see the soldiers with masks. We can see them getting off the vehicle. We also saw three people in the vehicle: Yourself and two other people. The vehicle that we saw looked like a military vehicle. Can you please confirm that this was indeed a military vehicle. What can you tell us about the vehicle that transported you to the place of exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't say it that this was a military vehicle. At that time, there were no military vehicles, typical military vehicles. I couldn't see the inside very well, and I didn't see how it was painted from the outside. I didn't see it from the outside at all. It was a civilian vehicle which had been requisitioned by the army. In most of the cases, there were all sorts of vehicles that were used by the army. I didn't see the registration plates on the vehicle, and I can't speak about the things I didn't see. I only know that there were soldiers in the vehicle and that I was brought there in that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. On the day of exchange, that vehicle that we could see on the tape, is that the vehicle that picked you up from the facility where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whenever I was taken out, I would be blindfolded. I would be put -- a bag on the head. I didn't see anything. The first time they took that bag off was when we arrived. When I was taken out from the vehicle, I believe that they kept me in the primary school on the day of exchange. I could have a glimpse of some children around. That's all I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. My question was very precise: When you were in the vehicle, between the place where you were detained and the place where you were exchanged, did you use just one vehicle or were there various vehicles involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one vehicle, from the place where I spent the last night to the place I was exchanged. I was not transferred from one vehicle to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question: When you entered the vehicle in order to be transported to the place of exchange, the soldiers who were in the vehicle were those who guarded you in detention or were they some other soldiers, soldiers who arrived in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know who they were, who were the guards. They were all in uniforms and they were all masked, so I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Withopf, you may proceed. We are going to give you an exhibit number for this tape that you're going to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P70, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you already mentioned yesterday that you had a meeting or that you met Mr. Dzemal Merdan in 1994. Was there any occasion at which Mr. Dzemal Merdan, who was, as you testified, the ABiH 3rd Corps deputy commander at the time, did Dzemal Merdan at any point in time make any reference to your kidnapping and/or your detention? Did he talk to you about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we avoided that. The BH army representatives avoided that topic. Although, I insisted on several occasions. However, during the negotiations at the military executive committee in Gornji Vakuf and in Uskoplje, around the 1st of March, 1994, after one meeting there, when we agreed to disagree on an issue - I believe that the issue was the separation line between the forces in Busovaca - he stood up. We were sitting around a table. There was a large map on the table. He stood up and said, "Why didn't we kill you when we had you in our hands?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have completed your examination-in-chief. Before I give the floor to the Defence, I would like to ask for some clarification that the Chamber might find useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were kidnapped, do you think that this kidnapping was planned well ahead and was it done with the ultimate objective of you being exchanged or was that a random kidnapping? As a soldier, can you answer? What was the reason for kidnapping? Were you kidnapped in order to be exchanged? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to what happened at the place where I was kidnapped and later on during the detention and during the exchange, the treatment that I was given made me conclude already on the first day -- actually, on the first day, I was in doubt. I was still afraid that I might be killed when they poured oil on me to stop bleeding. I knew that this was the way to stop bleeding. When I was detained, they told me that I was not a problem, that they only wanted me for exchange, that they wanted to capture the highest ranking officer, and they believed that I would be the one that would serve to exchange all of their Muslim brethren in prison. And the food that I was given, I would be wrong to say that this food was bad. I didn't suffer. I was kicked only once by a soldier. I was taunted. I was verbally threatened, but nobody ever maltreated me. Secondly, their treatment was very professional. When I was taken for exchange, they put boots on me and they laced my boots. They wanted me to look the part. Further on, some 30 days into my detention, a person came. He took off his mask. He was very polite, looked like a diplomat. He was a foreigner. He was very civilised. He asked me whether I was beaten. Then I said that I was kicked only once. And he asked me if I had been beaten. He wanted to know what was the date when this was done. And then he told me that it was not according to the Islam teachings to beat prisoners, that this shouldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. And the wound that you had, that was the wound that was a gunshot wound. Was that a surface wound or was that a slight injury? What would you say? You said that -- what was the nature of this wound? We did not understand the nature of that wound.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, whether this was a gunshot wound. I only know that I was hit with a rifle butt when I tried to get out of the vehicle. I don't know whether I was shot or not, because I was in a state of shock. However, there was a huge impact when the vehicle hit something some kilometre or so into our journey. I was sitting in the front. My hands were handcuffed in the back. There was a blanket over my body, and there was a bucket on my legs and one bucket on my shoulders. I had to lie down with that bag on my head. At one moment I felt an impact because the vehicle hit something, and I bumped into something in the vehicle. I don't know whether I was injured during the kidnapping or while I was in the vehicle. When the vehicle hit something, my glasses were broken. And I asked somebody during the journey to remove any glasses. I was afraid that the shattered glass could cut my eye. There was a lot of shattered glass on my face. The wound itself was somewhat deeper. It was half a centimetre deep. However, they gave me some medication, some powder. When they brought the first pill, I didn't want to swallow it. I was afraid that they wanted to poison me on that first day. However, later on one of them brought a prescription and told me what was prescribed to me, and he told me, "If you don't believe that this is an antibiotic, look at the prescription and see for yourself that we are giving you proper medicine," and that's when I started taking antibiotics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm turning to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Totic. My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, some of my questions will be general and some of the questions will be put to the witness to check the witness's credibility. Other questions will have to do with issues raised by the Prosecution in the course of his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, until recently you were a professional military man by profession; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1997, Your Honours, I was a professional soldier. In 1997, on the 1st of October, I joined the Ministry of Defence as a member of the military. But in the Ministry of Defence my professional life is suspended.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 26th of April, 1996 you left your position -- you said that on the 4th of December, 1991, after a certain training you came to Bihac, which is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. From the western part, not far from the Croatian border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, 1992, when you left the JNA, you went to fetch your family in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 26th, since I lived in Sarajevo and worked in Bihac, I got my family out on the 15th of April. I got them out of Sarajevo. That was the last time I -- they found accommodation with their parents and I went to work in Bihac. And up until -- and on the 26th, I went to Zenica, not to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you got to Zenica - that's the 26th of April - Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been internationally recognised as a state; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the JNA and the Serbian forces on the 6th of April, to be more precise, had already attacked Sarajevo, the main town -- the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct? On the 6th of April, when the town was liberated.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. All I know is that after the first barricades had been erected in Sarajevo, in Grbavica on the 20th of March, I think, I then decided to get my family out. I don't think the fighting had started at that time, but they had started putting up barricades in the town and there was sporadic shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to insist on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to the question you put to the witness, the witness's answer wasn't audible. The question concerned the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He didn't answer the question. Could you ask the witness the question again. It's line 7. In English, there is no audible response.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that on the 26th of April, when you left the JNA, Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been internationally recognised as a state?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, on the 26th of April, 1992 they declared a state of an imminent threat of war and all officers were called to report to the Territorial Defence Staff to organise the Defence of the country; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were two formations that had been legally formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll continue to ask you about those matters too. You previously said that in the former SFRY the Territorial Defence, in addition to the JNA, was part of the armed forces of the SFRY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct so say that the JNA, when it attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina, in fact ceased to be its armed forces and the Territorial Defence is what remained of the former armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't answer this question by simply saying yes or no. After the attack carried out by the former JNA against Bosnia and Herzegovina, and prior to the attack, the JNA was gradually ceasing to be the armed forces of the former SFRY and it was becoming a national force. But when it attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence, as the other armed component of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, became to a large extent a force of a single nation. It mostly consisted of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence before the war was a military structure which reflected the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, after the war, the legally elected leadership, the Presidency, and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were multi-ethnic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But after the withdrawal of the Serbian representatives, it became less and less multi-ethnic. You know very well that some people were elected by the Serbian people and that they withdrew; others were appointed. I won't go into that. These are political issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence command that the Presidency had declared as the legal Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina also reflected the multi-ethnic composition of the country; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the composition of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the staff commander at the beginning was Hasan Efendic, a Muslim, a Bosniak, and his deputies were Stjepan Siber, a Croat; and Jovan Divjak, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Jerko Doko, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you were a professional soldier and although you had a flat in Sarajevo, summons received by the Territorial Defence Staff was one that you didn't respond to. You didn't report to the Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was in Sarajevo. I had a flat there. I was born in Zenica. I didn't respond to the summons to go to the Republican Staff in Sarajevo for a simple reason: The flat in which I lived upon that occasion at that time and which I live now, I only got it back in 2001, in January 2001. It was in the part of town that immediately fell into Serbian hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, you said you reached Zenica. Zenica is in fact the largest city in Central Bosnia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If Sarajevo isn't taken to be in central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The population of the town was ethnically mixed; although, the majority were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to discuss this issue in greater detail. The ethnic composition of Zenica -- or rather, of the municipality of Zenica in 1991, it's true to say that 44.7 per cent were Bosniaks, 16.8 per cent were Serbs, and 15.6 per cent were Croats, and 16 per cent were others. Among the others, most of them had declared themselves as Yugoslavs. However, after the failure of the Territorial Defence forces when defending Eastern and Western Bosnia, many refugees arrived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, I'll be asking you about that. We're still talking about the prewar period. Zenica, as an industrial, an economical place, there were no conflicts of an ethnic kind in Zenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Zenica, as the Defence says, was inhabited by various ethnic groups, and you could say that these ethnic groups lived in harmony together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, after the war -- I mean, after the beginning of the war, after the Serbian forces had occupied important areas of Krajina and Eastern Bosnia, tens of thousands of refugees expelled from Eastern Bosnia and Krajina arrived in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, between 35.000 and 40.000 arrived, and they were mostly Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: About 90 per cent of the refugees were Muslims or Bosniaks. One could say that that was the case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That fact significantly changed the ethnic composition of the population in Zenica, and as a result we could say that towards the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993 about 80 per cent of the population was Bosniak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I couldn't say, because that's just one aspect. The arrival of refugees is one aspect. And the second aspect has to do with the attack of the Territorial Defence forces in May and clearing up the Drivusa village. After that event, the message -- a clear message was sent to the Serbs. In fact, the Serbs after that event ran away from Zenica. There were over 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After a number of general questions I have put to you - and you were able to answer them - I will now go back to the part of your testimony that concerned the time when you were kidnapped in Zenica in mid-April 1993. Would it be true to say that on several occasions you have given statements about your kidnapping and you have testified about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I testified about it on only one occasion, and that was before this Tribunal in the Dario Kordic case, as a witness for the Defence. As far as giving statements are concerned, I gave a statement. I was the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and there was the president Dario Kordic and Anto Valenta, who were political figures at the time. And I gave a statement in 1994 or 1995 to representatives of the authorised organs of the military police and to the district public prosecutor, because at the time I thought that this should be looked into. But I didn't testify before any other courts, apart from this court here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that when you were detained, you found out from someone that your kidnapping had been carried out by a special military police unit from the 3rd Corps. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. But I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, what you heard when in detention is a very important factor for you, and that is why you mentioned it before the Court today.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to inform the Chamber of everything that I have heard about while in detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have just said that for your own needs and the needs of your commanders, for the needs of Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic and Anto Valenta, you made a report, I would like this report to be shown to the witness. We have a sufficient number of copies for the Trial Chamber and for our colleagues. We received this report in the pre-trial period from the Prosecution. Have a look at it, please. Is that the report that you made after you had been exchanged? Did you give it to your commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my commanders but to my commander. And these are two political figures. But Mr. Dario Kordic had the rank of colonel at the time. But I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, is it correct to say that on the 13th of October, 1993 you wrote a report for the needs of the Centre for Human Rights, which Anto Damjanovic took down? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since my questions will relate to both statements, could this statement also be shown to the Witness. We received it from the Prosecution, and it contains the witness's handwritten text and the text that has been typed out and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, is this the report that you yourself wrote?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this isn't my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign these statements?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see my signature either. I know Mr. Anto Damjanovic. I'm aware of the fact that he worked for the Centre for Human Rights. I know that at the time he worked in some sort of a service. I have spoken about this matter. This isn't my handwriting, and the signature is illegible. I can't confirm that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the handwritten text, there is a signature on each page. Can you recognise your own signature on those pages?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only recognise my signature here, at the end, on the last page. But on the other pages, no, I can't see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in 1993, in October, you spoke about this subject, and the person you spoke to made a record of what you said; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was an authorised official from the security service at the time. I spoke about the subject privately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you sign anything that was recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I put my signature on the last page, but at the time there was no electricity because there was a general attack underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the usher to give a better copy of this statement to the witness. At the bottom of each page the signature is much more legible, so I'm going to ask the witness to see whether he can recognise his signature on this copy here.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this should be my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. We have identified the statement. You didn't write it in your own hand but you did sign it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you several questions about the two documents that I have just given you. These are reports to your commander and vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, i.e., its secretary, and these were the first statements that you gave after the exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Anto also read it when I gave my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also on the 3rd of May, 2000 gave certain information which were used by the Kordic Defence and Blaskic Defence in those trials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified as a Defence witness in the Kordic case before this Tribunal. It was in the year 2000, not in 1999, as you stated yesterday. You got confused on that.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said I wasn't sure whether it was in 1999 or in 2000. In any case, it was in April or in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, in March 2001 you gave a statement to the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Commander Blaskic and other political figures, you also spoke about the persons who carried out your kidnapping. So I would kindly ask you -- again your answer was not recorded. The question was whether in March 2001 you gave a statement to the OTP. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it, but it wasn't recorded, and only the things that are recorded can be considered your answers. Thank you for repeating your answer in this case. I'm going to ask you to look at the pages that I'm going to mention, and every time I'm going to also mention the date stated therein and the paragraph under that date. I'm not going to give you the numbers of paragraphs and the pages thereon, but I'm going to refer to the dates. Firstly, tell me, is it correct that in that statement you put the events in chronological order and described whatever happened to you during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from one day to another, from one date to another, I described events. However, I cannot be 100 per cent sure that I am right about the dates. I did not have a watch. It had been taken away from me. I didn't know the difference between the day and the night. The only way I could say that it was daylight is because I could hear the prayer invitation coming from a nearby mosque. I believed at the time that it was a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. You stated before this Trial Chamber that all the persons that communicated with you, with the exception of this Arab, were always masked; they wore masks on their faces.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all except the Arab, who wore a tunic. And before my exchange, another person came, whose name I don't know. He asked me questions about whether I had been beaten. And also, one of the escorts in the command who brought food, he was also an Arab. He was a guard. Towards the end of my stay there, he took his mask off and he told me that he was an Arab and he also told me that he could hardly wait to leave. "These are not Muslims. Women look differently here, and I can hardly wait for the day to leave here." So these were the three men that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April - page 2, paragraph 5, B/C/S version; and on the same page of the English version - you described the moment of the attack and you said that while he was putting a tape in the cassette player he shouted "An attack," ask then you saw a Volkswagen, a white Volkswagen and four people ran out of it -- out of the Audi. And there were two masked people who ran out of the Audi. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The road was blocked by the two vehicles and we couldn't proceed. I ordered the driver to try and avoid them, because there was a hill and we could maybe turn around and then go back towards the town. But it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in this report, also under the 15th of April, on paragraph 3, page 15 of the B/C/S version, you say and you describe the basement where you were brought to? You also say that you heard guards speaking in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I heard them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the entire text that you wrote you described the things that you testify about here. Firstly, that there were some political questions put to you and then that some people came and asked you some military questions? Is that something that you wrote down in your report?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that, as it says on the page describing the 16th of April - that is, page 3 in B/C/S, paragraph 4; and page 3, paragraph 4 of the English version, to the very bottom - once you were transferred to a different place, to a different room there were guards there, some ten of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I only wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that there's again no audible response of the witness in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Again I hear your answers, but apparently the interpreters can't hear you. Can you move closer to the microphone. Is it correct that they first asked you some political questions and then some military questions and that this is also stated in your report? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my last question about the 16th of April. In B/C/S, this is paragraph 4, page 3; and also paragraph 4, page 3 in the English version.
